newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: Bangui awaits mediator after fresh bloodshed.
newsitem.headline: Bangui awaits mediator after fresh bloodshed.

text.p: Mediator Amadou Toumani Toure headed back to the Central African Republic capital Bangui on Monday after three days of clashes between African peacekeepers and disaffected soldiers killed at least 30 people.

With the city enjoying a lull in the fighting after a night of shooting and mortar fire, Mali's widely respected former military leader expressed disappointment that a January peace deal had started to unravel again.

But he said any solution to the clashes, which stem from political and ethnic rivalry between supporters and opponents of President Ange-Felix Patasse within the army, lay with the Central African Republic citizens themselves.
"My role is to help the two parties, the different parties to agree," he told Radio France International in an interview. "The vital role will always come back to the nationals."
Residents said overnight shooting died down around dawn. "People who fled their homes are starting to return but timidly," one said. "Everyone is waiting for Toumani Toure. Hope rests on him."

The Bangui peacekeeping force has been touted as a model for a solution in Brazzaville, capital of the neighbouring Congo Republic when similar political and ethnic clashes killed hundreds of people this month.

Former colonial power France, which has troops stationed in Bangui under a defence pact, intervened on Sunday to defend the African peacekeepers, who deployed in the city under the January pact to end a third army mutiny in under a year.

"As part of support for the African force, French forces in Bangui became involved as part of self-defence to prevent firing at Senegalese and Chadian positions," General Jean-Pierre Perez told France's La Chaine Info television later.
Perez said the ex-mutineers had started firing mortars at Chadian and Senegalese peacekeepers on Sunday after a lull.
Witnesses said French helicopters flew over the city.
Around 70 people have been wounded in the fighting, including five French nationals who were hit on Saturday by two stray mortar bombs that fell on the French embassy compound.

The January 25 deal included a plan to reintegrate the mutineers into their units and then conduct general disarmament. Many mutineers had already rejoined their units but the process snagged this month on efforts to reintegrate members of the paramilitary gendarmerie.

Mutinies in April and May 1996 began as protests over pay but became a movement to topple Patasse, a northern civilian elected in 1993. The third mutiny began in November and degenerated into ethnic bloodshed.
Most of the mutineers are members of the Yakoma tribe of former military leader Andre Kolingba.
The French troops -- there are now 1,650 in the country -- restored order after the last mutiny and then handed over to the peacekeepers.
The 800-strong African force includes soldiers from Burkina Faso, Chad, Gabon, Mali, Senegal and Togo. A Senegalese soldier killed on Friday was among the first casualties of the flare-up.
